3. The defendants contested the suit and filed written statements contending, inter alia, that in view of the Bangladesh Bank Circular No. BCD (FI) 270/A-44 dated 7.9.83, the suit filed by the plaintiff was premature and not maintainable and that there was also no cause of action. The said circular clearly stipulated that the principal amount of outstanding dues as on 30.6.80 relating to the advance for the year 1979-80 by all the nationalised Banks, as was the case of the defendants, was to be repaid over a period of 5 years from 1983-84, penal interest relating to 1979-80 would be waived and no further interest would be charged and normal interest would also be charged only up to 30.12.82 and 50% of such interest would also be remitted and the borrower would be required only to pay the remaining 50% of the interest. The defendants wrote to the plaintiff for withdrawal of the case and for rescheduling the payment but though the proposal of the defendants was in accordance with the circular of Bangladesh Bank and hence endorsed by the plaintiff, the suit was not withdrawn. 

 11. Mr MA Tarek, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits that the grounds under which the plaint could be rejected being not present in the instant case the learned Subordinate Judge has committed no error of law in rejecting the prayer of the defendants for rejection of the plaint at the initial stage. 

 "11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases: 

 From the plain reading of the above provisions of the Code it appears that the plaint shall only be rejected if any one or more of the requirements of the aforesaid provisions is not fulfilled. Now, for the purpose of deciding whether the learned Court below is justified in passing the impugned order or not rule 11(a) and 11(d) of Order 7 of the Code are relevant. Rule 11(a) deals with the law relating to the rejection of plaint on the ground of non-disclosure of cause of action. When it is apparent on the fact of the plaint that if does not disclose any cause of action, it became a duty cast upon the Court to pass an order of rejection of the plaint but when it becomes necessary for the Court to arrive at the conclusion after consideration of the entire materials on record including evidence, oral and documentary, the Court is not under obligation to pass an order for rejection of the plaint at the earlier stage. The plea that there is no cause of action for the suit is different from saying that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action. In the former case there is scope for investigation as to whether the plaint is liable to be rejected and in the latter case it is the duty of the Court to reject the plaint at an earlier stage without entering into lengthy investigation. 

 15. It appears from the provision of Order 7 rule 11 of the Code that the plaint can be rejected only on any one or more of the live grounds mentioned there in before. The purpose of inserting these rules in the Code seems to be that a plaint should be rejected in its inception, if there is no cause of action, or if the suit is barred by any law so that no further time is consumed on the fruitless litigation causing unnecessary expenditure. The rule, therefore, lays down a duty upon the Court to examine the plaint to ascertain whether it is defective or whether it discloses any cause of action and, or, whether the suit is barred by any law. The provision of the rule is thus mandatory and the Court must discharge its responsibility in this respect with care and caution. The plaint could be rejected under this rule if the defects mentioned therein are apparent on the face of plaint. Before taking the measure of throwing the plaintiff out of court, the court should consider very carefully the nature of the defect in the plaint. In the instant case the rejection of the plaint was prayed for under the provision of clauses (a) and (b) of rule 11 of Order 7 of the Code. Clause (a) speaks of the non-disclosure of the cause of action in the plaint. According to this clause, the plaint which does not disclose any cause of action should be rejected. The phrase "cause of action" means the whole of the material facts which is necessary for the plaintiff to allege and prove in order to succeed in the suit. 

 16. Mr. MA Tarik has referred to the case of SK Md Junaid and others Vs. Turner Morrison and Co. Ltd. reported in 26 DLR 111 wherein the learned judges placing reliance on a number of decisions of this Court and other High Courts of Indian Jurisdiction held "the power of rejection of a plaint under rule 11 shall be exercised only if the Court comes to the conclusion on mere reading of the plaint that even if all the allegations are proved the plaintiff would not be entitled to any relief whatsoever." Thus the power of rejection of a plaint under rule 11 of Order 7 shall, therefore, be exercised if the Court comes to the conclusion on mere reading of the plaint that all the allegations, if proved, the plaintiff would "not be entitled to any relief whatsoever". It is further held in the said case: In considering the question of cause of action, the court shall apply its mind to the averments in the plaint and not to any other matte and in so doing it shall presume every allegation made in the plaint as true" Mr. Tarik further submits that the defendants have failed to discharge their burden by showing that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action and hence is liable to be rejected in limine. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the opposite party has referred to the case of Moose Vs. Mohamed and others reported in PLD 1954 Sind page 70 and the case of Sankarrao Balaji and others Vs. Shambihari and others reported in AIR 1951 (Nag) 419 and the case of Thounaojam Nigal Indrani Devi and others Vs. Municipal Board of Imphal and others reported in AIR 1958 (Manipur) 27. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, on the other hand, submit that the cause of action which was said to have been there at the time of filing of the suit ceased to exist on the issuance of the Bangladesh Bank's Circular by which five years' time was given to the defendant for liquidating the loan money and in that view of the matter the suit should not have been allowed to proceed during that period. Thus there was no denial of the fact that cause of action was there at the time of filing the suit and by the Bangladesh Bank's circular the borrowers have not been absolved of their liability but privilege was given to them by way of extending time for repaying the loan and penal interest was remitted. We are, therefore, of the view that the cause of action which arose before the filing of the suit has not ceased altogether, rather subsists and, therefore, the plaint is not liable to be rejected on the ground of cause of action. Now the question remains to be decided as to whether the suit is barred by law and hence the plaint is liable to be rejected under clause (d) of rule 11 of Order 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Circular issued by the Bangladesh Bank has not created any embargo or bar in filing a suit for the realisation of money. The allegations made and the relief claimed in the plaint also do not bring the suit within the mischief of the clause (d) of rule 11 of Order 7 of the Code so as to render the suit barred by any law. In the case of Maqzood Ali Vs. Deputy Commissioner Bara Banki and another reported in AIR 1928 (Oudh) 495 a Division Bench of Oudh High Court held that if the suit was on the face of it not barred by any law, Order 7 rule 11 (d) of the Code had no application. In the case of Sreedam Chandra Bhur Vs. Tinkori Mukharjee and others reported in AIR 1953 (Cal) 222 it was held that Order 7 rule 11 (d) was attracted only when on the admitted facts appearing in the plaint the suit was prima facie barred. In the instant case there is nothing to show that on the admitted facts as appearing from the plaint itself the suit is prima facie barred. There is also nothing in the circular from which it can be said that the suit filed claiming the repayment of the loan money by the borrower will be barred. Therefore, it must be found, and we accept the view, that the rules 11 (a) and 11 (d) of Order 7 of the Code have no manner of application in the instant case and the plaint is not liable to be rejected on that score. Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud further contends that in case the suit cannot be brought within the mischief of Order 7 rule 11 of the Code the Court has the power to reject the plaint by exercising his discretionary power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and, in support of his contention, he has referred to the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd Vs. Burmah Employees Union re-ported in PLD 1967, (Dha) 190. In the said case the Court was found to have exercised its discretionary power under section 151 of the Code in the absence of any specific provision of law. The Court, of course, can exercise such discretion if defect is found apparent on the face of the plaint and said defect is so fatal and perilous that interference of the Court is necessary. Generally, the Court does not exercise such power because the Court is to keep in view the interest of not only the petitioner but also the interest of the 'other party, who may be affected thereby. We do not find that such circumstances exist in the present case calling for the rejection of the plaint at this stage invoking the aid of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case it appears that the suit was filed with the positive averments in the plaint regarding the cause of action which was in existence at the time of filing of suit and the plaint suffers from no laches or defect within the meaning of Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it cannot be said that the cause of action which was there at the time of filing of the suit has ceased to exist within the meaning of rule 11 (a) of Order 7 or the suit has become barred by any law so as to bring it within the ambit of and to be dealt with under Order 7 rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. There being no inherent defect on the face of the record rejection of the plaint by invoking the aid of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure was also not called for. 

 17. For the aforesaid reasons we find that the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have committed no error of law in his decision occasioning failure of justice in disallowing the prayer for rejection of the plaint. As we do not find that the impugned order suffers from any legal defect, we do not consider it a fit case for our interference at this stage. 

 Let the order of stay earlier passed in the case be vacated.
